Different authorities propose slightly different values, particularly for the intermediate Śrutis within each svara's range.)

The Four Śrutis of Sa

The tonic (Sa) is assigned 4 Śrutis. This might seem paradoxical — isn't Sa a single, fixed pitch? — but it reflects a profound understanding:

  1. Sa is not absolutely fixed. The precise pitch of Sa varies from performer to performer, from instrument to instrument, from context to context. The 4 Śrutis of Sa represent the range of acceptable variation — the "bandwidth" within which Sa can be intoned while still functioning as a stable tonic.

  2. The 4 Śrutis encode the four stages of sound. Just as Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī represent four levels of sonic manifestation, the 4 Śrutis of Sa represent four levels of tonic presence — from the subtlest, most internalized hearing of Sa (Tīvrā = "intense," the inner awareness of the tonic) to the most externalized, most fully sounded Sa (Chandovatī = "rhythmic," the fully manifest tonic that establishes the metrical framework of the performance).

  3. The 4 Śrutis correspond to the 4 puruṣārthas. Dharma (righteousness), Artha (prosperity), Kāma (desire), and Mokṣa (liberation) — the four goals of human life — are encoded in the four Śrutis of the tonic. The tonic is the microcosm of the entire human enterprise; its four Śrutis represent the full range of human aspiration.

The Two Śrutis of Ga and Ni

Ga and Ni have only 2 Śrutis each, making them the most emotionally sensitive svaras. With less tonal "space" to move in, every slight change in the intonation of Ga or Ni produces a dramatic change in emotional quality. This is why:

  • Ga is the svara that most powerfully distinguishes major from minor (in Western terms). The two Śrutis of Ga correspond roughly to the major third (Krodhā, Śruti 9) and the minor third (Raudrī, Śruti 8). The difference between these two positions — a single Śruti — is the difference between joy and sorrow, between brightness and shadow.

  • Ni is the svara that most powerfully determines the "flavor" of the upper tetrachord. The two Śrutis of Ni correspond roughly to the major seventh (Kṣobhiṇī, Śruti 22) and the minor seventh (Ugrā, Śruti 21). The major seventh creates tension, aspiration, yearning for resolution; the minor seventh creates depth, mystery, introspection.

In Dīkṣitar's compositions, the treatment of Ga and Ni is often the signature of the rāga's therapeutic intention. In rāgas with Antara Gāndhāra (G3, the high Ga), the healing quality tends toward brightness, confidence, and energizing. In rāgas with Sādhāraṇa Gāndhāra (G2, the middle Ga), the quality tends toward warmth, empathy, and emotional connection. In rāgas with Śuddha Gāndhāra (G1, the low Ga), the quality tends toward introversion, contemplation, and deep stillness.

Chapter 2.3: Mathematical Ratios and Frequency Relationships

Pages 63��68

The Mathematics of Consonance

The 22 Śrutis are not arbitrarily placed along the octave. They are determined by specific mathematical ratios — relationships between frequencies that the human ear perceives as consonant, dissonant, or neutral.

The fundamental consonances are:

Interval Ratio Śruti Position Quality
Unison 1:1 Sa (Śruti 1) Perfect identity
Octave 2:1 Upper Sa Perfect completion
Perfect Fifth 3:2 Pa (Śruti 14) Perfect harmony
Perfect Fourth 4:3 Ma (Śruti 10) Perfect grounding
Major Third 5:4 Ga (Śruti 9) Sweet brightness
Minor Third 6:5 Ga (Śruti 8) Gentle pathos
Major Sixth 5:3 Dha (Śruti 20) Warm beauty
Minor Sixth 8:5 Dha (Śruti 19) Deep emotion
Major Second 9:8 or 10:9 Re (Śruti 7 or 6) Forward movement
Minor Second 16:15 Re (Śruti 5) Tension, yearning
Major Seventh 15:8 Ni (Śruti 22) Aspiration
Minor Seventh 16:9 Ni (Śruti 21) Depth

The Two Generating Principles

The 22 Śrutis can be generated by two complementary mathematical processes:

1. The Cycle of Fifths: Starting from Sa, ascending by perfect fifths (ratio 3:2) and bringing each resulting note back within the octave (by halving its frequency as many times as necessary), generates a series of tones. After 12 such steps, you arrive close to the starting Sa — but not exactly. The difference (the "Pythagorean comma") is approximately 23.46 cents. This process generates the Pythagorean or cyclical version of the Śrutis.

2. The Harmonic Series: The natural overtones of any vibrating body — the 2nd harmonic (octave), 3rd (fifth), 4th (double octave), 5th (major third two octaves up), 6th (fifth an octave up), 7th (minor seventh), etc. — provide a different set of ratios. These are the just intonation or harmonic Śrutis, characterized by the pure, beatless quality of their intervals.

The Indian 22-Śruti system incorporates both generating principles. Some Śrutis are best understood as products of the cycle of fifths (particularly the Śrutis of Sa, Ma, and Pa); others are best understood as products of the harmonic series (particularly the Śrutis of Ga, Dha, and Ni). The system as a whole represents a synthesis of cyclical and harmonic thinking — a mathematical map of all the important frequency relationships that the human ear can perceive.

Healing Implications of Mathematical Ratios

The mathematical ratios of the Śrutis are not merely abstract numbers. They are prescriptions for specific vibratory experiences:

  • Simple ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3) produce consonant intervals that the nervous system experiences as restful, harmonious, and integrating. These ratios are associated with the sattvic (pure, balanced) quality and are therapeutic for conditions involving agitation, fragmentation, and disharmony — anxiety, ADHD, insomnia, hypertension.

  • Moderately complex ratios (5:4, 6:5, 5:3, 8:5) produce sweet intervals that the nervous system experiences as emotionally moving, beautiful, and satisfying. These ratios are associated with the rajasic (active, passionate) quality in its positive form and are therapeutic for conditions involving emotional blockage, depression, and lack of motivation.

  • Highly complex ratios (9:8, 10:9, 16:15, 15:8, 16:9) produce tense intervals that the nervous system experiences as stimulating, challenging, and energizing. These ratios are associated with the rajasic quality in its more intense form and are therapeutic for conditions involving lethargy, stagnation, and kapha accumulation.

The 72 Melakarta system organizes these ratios into 72 distinct therapeutic profiles, each with its own balance of consonance, sweetness, and tension. This is the subject of Section III.

Chapter 2.4: The Two Śruti Traditions: Cyclical and Harmonic

Pages 69–73

The Pythagorean (Cyclical) Approach

In this approach, all intervals are derived from the cycle of perfect fifths (3:2 ratio). Starting from Sa:

scss

Copy code

Sa → Pa (3:2) → Re (9:8) → Dha (27:16) → Ga (81:64) → Ni (243:128) → Ma# (729:512)...

Each step multiplies the previous frequency by 3/2, then divides by 2 if necessary to stay within the octave. This generates a set of intervals with the following properties:

  • All fifths are pure (exactly 3:2)

  • All fourths are pure (exactly 4:3)

  • Thirds are slightly wide (81:64 instead of 5:4 for the major third)

  • The system is internally consistent but slightly "sharp" relative to natural harmonics

Healing quality of Pythagorean intervals: These intervals are bright, clear, angular, and structuring. They appeal to the intellect and the sense of order. They are therapeutic for conditions involving mental confusion, lack of discipline, and structural disorganization.

Dīkṣitar's compositions in rāgas that emphasize the Sa-Pa axis (rāgas with prominent use of the perfect fifth) tend to have a Pythagorean quality — bright, architecturally precise, intellectually satisfying.

The Harmonic (Just Intonation) Approach

In this approach, intervals are derived from the natural harmonic series — the overtones that any vibrating body produces:

java

Run CodeCopy code

Fundamental (1:1 = Sa) 2nd harmonic (2:1 = Upper Sa) 3rd harmonic (3:2 = Pa) 4th harmonic (4:3 → Ma by inversion) 5th harmonic (5:4 = Ga "pure major third") 6th harmonic (6:5 → Ga "pure minor third" via different derivation) 7th harmonic (7:4 → Ni "natural seventh")

This generates intervals that are:

  • Beatless (perfectly consonant, with no audible interference patterns)

  • Warm and resonant

  • "Natural" in quality — the ear recognizes them immediately as consonant

Healing quality of harmonic intervals: These intervals are warm, resonant, enveloping, and emotionally moving. They appeal to the heart and the emotions. They are therapeutic for conditions involving emotional coldness, disconnection, alienation, and lack of empathy.

Śyāma Śāstri's compositions, with their characteristic emotional warmth and their emphasis on the expressive potential of Ga and Ni, tend to have a harmonic-just-intonation quality — warm, resonant, heart-opening.

The Indian Synthesis

The genius of the 22-Śruti system is that it includes both Pythagorean and harmonic intervals within a single framework. This allows the Indian musician to choose, moment by moment, between the bright clarity of Pythagorean intonation and the warm resonance of harmonic intonation — or to blend the two in various proportions.

This flexibility is one of the sources of Indian music's extraordinary therapeutic range. A rāga performed with primarily Pythagorean Śrutis will have a different healing quality than the same rāga performed with primarily harmonic Śrutis. The skilled performer — and the skilled Rāga Cikitsā practitioner — adjusts the Śruti values to match the therapeutic need of the listener.

Chapter 2.5: Śruti and Bhāva: How Microtones Create Emotional States

Pages 74–78

The Śruti-Bhāva Connection

Bhāva (भाव) — literally "being" or "becoming" — refers in musical and theatrical contexts to the specific emotional state evoked by a performance. The Nāṭyaśāstra identifies eight (later nine) primary bhāvas or rasas:

Rasa Meaning Dominant Śruti Region
Śṛṅgāra Love/Beauty Ga (8-9), Ni (21-22): sweet thirds and sevenths
Hāsya Humor/Joy Re (6-7), Dha (19-20): bright seconds and sixths
Karuṇa Compassion/Sorrow Ga (8), Ni (21): minor thirds and sevenths
Raudra Anger/Ferocity All sharp/tense intervals
Vīra Heroism/Courage Sa (1-4), Pa (14-17): strong tonic and fifth
Bhayānaka Fear/Terror Ga (8), Dha (18): diminished intervals
Bībhatsa Disgust/Aversion Dissonant combinations
Adbhuta Wonder/Amazement Unusual Śruti combinations
Śānta Peace/Tranquility Sa (1), Pa (14): pure consonances

The relationship between Śruti values and emotional states is not arbitrary. It is grounded in the psychoacoustic properties of intervals:

  • Consonant intervals (small-number ratios) are perceived as stable, restful, and peaceful → Śānta rasa

  • Moderately dissonant intervals (medium-number ratios) are perceived as emotionally moving, tender, and bittersweet → Śṛṅgāra and Karuṇa rasas

  • Strongly dissonant intervals (large-number ratios) are perceived as tense, energetic, and challenging → Raudra and Vīra rasas

How Dīkṣitar Uses Śruti for Bhāva

Dīkṣitar's genius lies in his ability to create precise emotional effects through precise Śruti choices. Consider his kṛti "Mīnākṣī me mudam dehi" (Rāga Gamakakriyā, Melakarta 53):

Rāga Gamakakriyā uses: Sa, R1, G3, M2, Pa, D1, N3

The combination of R1 (low Re, Śruti 5 — Dayāvatī, "compassionate") with G3 (high Ga, Śruti 9 — Krodhā, "fierce") creates a wide interval between the second and third degrees — an interval that conveys yearning, stretching, aspiration. This perfectly matches the sāhitya's content: "Mīnākṣī, give me bliss" — the devotee stretching toward the Goddess, yearning for her grace.

The M2 (Prati Madhyama) adds a note of sharpness and urgency — the yearning is not passive but active, insistent, passionate.

The D1 (low Dha, Śruti 18 — Madantī, "intoxicating") combined with N3 (high Ni, Śruti 22 — Kṣobhiṇī, "agitating") creates a similar wide interval in the upper tetrachord, mirroring the lower tetrachord's yearning quality and establishing a whole-octave therapeutic field of aspiration and grace.

How Śyāma Śāstri Uses Śruti for Bhāva

Śyāma Śāstri's approach is different but equally precise. Consider his masterpiece "O Jagadambā" (Rāga Ānandabhairavī):

Rāga Ānandabhairavī (a janya of Melakarta 20, Naṭabhairavī) uses: Sa, R2, G2, Ma, Pa, D2, N2

This scale is rich in middle-position Śrutis — R2 (Śruti 6, Ranjanī, "pleasing"), G2 (Śruti 8, Raudrī, "fierce" — but in context, "poignant"), D2 (Śruti 19, Rohiṇī, "growing"), N2 (Śruti 21, Ugrā, "powerful"). The overall Śruti profile is one of moderate tension with emotional warmth — not the bright clarity of major-mode rāgas, not the deep darkness of highly dissonant rāgas, but a twilight quality — tender, vulnerable, infinitely human.

This Śruti profile perfectly supports the sāhitya: "O Mother of the universe!" — the cry of a child to its mother, simultaneously powerful and vulnerable, demanding and surrendering. The "moderate tension" of the intervals creates the space for emotional catharsis — the listener can feel the devotee's pain, participate in it, and then experience the release that comes when the Goddess responds.

Chapter 2.6: Śruti in Dīkṣitar's Compositions: Microtonal Mastery in Practice

Pages 79–83

Dīkṣitar's Microtonal Signature

Dīkṣitar's compositions are distinguished by an extraordinary attention to Śruti — an attention that reflects his training in Vedic chanting, his knowledge of mantra śāstra, and his deep understanding of the healing properties of specific frequency ratios.

Several features characterize Dīkṣitar's Śruti practice:

1. Extended Gamaka (Oscillation): Dīkṣitar's melodic style features long, slow oscillations around each note — the note is not attacked directly but approached from below or above, touched, sustained with gentle vibrato, and then released. This gamaka technique ensures that the full Śruti range of each note is explored, activating all the microtonal healing properties associated with that note's Śruti region.

2. Kampita (Shake): A specific type of gamaka in which the note oscillates rapidly between two adjacent Śrutis. This kampita creates a shimmer effect — the note seems to glow or vibrate with an inner light. Therapeutically, kampita activates the nervous system at a very subtle level, producing a state of alert relaxation that is ideal for healing.

3. Śruti-Sāhitya Alignment: Dīkṣitar carefully aligns the emotional weight of the Sanskrit syllable with the Śruti weight of the note. Heavy, resonant syllables (those with anusvāra, long vowels, or compound consonants) are placed on notes with strong Śruti presence (Sa, Ma, Pa); light, agile syllables are placed on notes with delicate Śruti presence (Ga, Ni). This alignment creates a phonemic-musical coherence that amplifies the healing effect of both the text and the melody.

Case Study: "Akṣayaliṅga Vibho" (Rāga Śaṅkarābharaṇam, Melakarta 29)

This kṛti, addressed to Śiva in the form of the Akṣayaliṅga at Tiruvārūr, is one of Dīkṣitar's most celebrated compositions. Let us examine its Śruti profile:

Rāga Śaṅkarābharaṇam (Melakarta 29): Sa, R2, G3, M1, Pa, D2, N3

This is the Indian equivalent of the Western major scale — the brightest, most balanced, most universally appealing of all scales. Its Śruti profile is:

  • Sa (Śrutis 1-4): Full, stable tonic — grounding

  • R2 (Śruti 7, Rati, "pleasure"): Warm, pleasant second — comforting

  • G3 (Śruti 9, Krodhā): In this context, not "angry" but bright and confident — the major third radiating sunlight

  • M1 (Śruti 13, Mārjanī, "purifying"): The pure, natural fourth — cleansing

  • Pa (Śrutis 14-17): Full, stable fifth — harmonizing

  • D2 (Śruti 20, Ramyā, "beautiful"): The warm, beautiful sixth — soothing

  • N3 (Śruti 22, Kṣobhiṇī): The leading tone, creating gentle upward aspiration — elevating

The overall therapeutic profile is one of comprehensive balance — grounding and elevating, comforting and energizing, purifying and beautifying. Śaṅkarābharaṇam is the rāga-equivalent of a broad-spectrum tonic — it addresses the whole person, bringing every aspect of body, mind, and soul into alignment.

The sāhitya "Akṣayaliṅga Vibho" means "O Lord of the Imperishable Liṅga" — identifying Śiva with the eternal, indestructible principle of consciousness. The Sanskrit word "Akṣaya" (imperishable) contains:

  • A (the primordial vowel, activating the throat and chest)

  • Kṣ (the compound consonant, activating the palate and back of the mouth)

  • a (again, open vowel)

  • ya (palatal glide, activating the palate)

This sequence of sounds — open, compound, open, glide — creates a phonemic pattern that opens, contracts, opens, and flows — mirroring the pattern of breathing and the pattern of the heartbeat. The word itself becomes a miniature Prāṇāyāma, a micro-rhythmic exercise that entrains the singer's breath and heartbeat to its pattern.

Combined with the Śruti profile of Śaṅkarābharaṇam, the result is a comprehensive healing experience — the body is tuned by the Śrutis, the breath is entrained by the sāhitya, the mind is focused by the rāga's clarity, and the soul is awakened by the invocation of Śiva.

Case Study: Navagraha Kṛtis — Planetary Healing

Dīkṣitar's nine Navagraha Kṛtis represent the most explicit Rāga Cikitsā in the Carnatic repertoire. Each kṛti invokes a specific planet (graha) in a specific rāga chosen for its planetary correspondence:

Planet Kṛti Rāga Melakarta Śruti Profile Healing Target
Sūrya (Sun) Sūryamūrte Saurāṣṭram Janya of 17 Bright, warm Vitality, eyesight, heart
Candra (Moon) Candram bhaja Asāveri Janya of 8 Soft, cooling Emotions, sleep, fluids
Maṅgala (Mars) Aṅgārakam Surāṭi Janya of 28 Sharp, energetic Courage, blood, muscles
Budha (Mercury) Budham āśraye Nāṭakuranji Janya of 28 Quick, flexible Intelligence, speech, nerves
Guru (Jupiter) Bṛhaspate Athāṇā Janya of 29 Expansive, benevolent Wisdom, liver, fat tissue
Śukra (Venus) Śukra bhagavantam Pharas Janya of 22 Sweet, beautiful Love, kidneys, reproduction
Śani (Saturn) Divākara tanujam Yādukula Kāmbhoji Janya of 28 Heavy, structured Bones, discipline, longevity
Rāhu Smarāmi anisham Rāmamanohārī Janya of 52 Unusual, mysterious Obsessions, psychic disturbances
Ketu Mahāsuram ketum Cāmaram Janya of 28 Detaching, liberating Spiritual liberation, past karma

Each kṛti is traditionally prescribed for periods when the corresponding planet is afflicted in the individual's horoscope. The combination of the rāga's Śruti profile, the Sanskrit mantra's phonemic properties, and the devotional invocation of the planet creates a targeted astrological-musical remedy that addresses the specific body systems, psychological tendencies, and karmic patterns associated with that planet.

This is Rāga Cikitsā at its most systematic and most explicit — music as planetary medicine, Sanskrit as astrological mantra, the 22 Śrutis as therapeutic frequencies calibrated to cosmic rhythms.

Chapter 2.7: Śruti in Śyāma Śāstri's Compositions: The Weeping Intervals

Pages 84–87

The Emotional Precision of Śyāma Śāstri

If Dīkṣitar is the cosmic healer, Śyāma Śāstri is the heart healer. His compositions specialize in the Karuṇa rasa — the aesthetic emotion of compassion, tenderness, and gentle sorrow — and his use of Śruti is directed toward creating precisely calibrated emotional states that facilitate catharsis and emotional release.

The "Weeping Intervals"

Śyāma Śāstri's compositions frequently employ what we might call "weeping intervals" — specific Śruti combinations that the human nervous system responds to with an impulse toward tears, tenderness, and emotional opening. These include:

  1. The minor third (Raudrī, Śruti 8): This interval, slightly narrower than the Western minor third, has a quality of poignant sweetness — not despair, but the tenderness that arises when the heart is open and vulnerable.

  2. The minor seventh (Ugrā, Śruti 21): This interval creates a sense of depth and longing — the feeling of looking into a deep well, or gazing at a distant horizon. It is not sad, exactly, but spacious — it creates room for emotions that normally have no room.

  3. The flat second (Dayāvatī, Śruti 5): This interval, barely a semitone above Sa, creates a quality of intimate closeness — as if the melody is whispering a secret, leaning in close, sharing something too tender for ordinary speech.

  4. The combination of flat second with minor third: This is Śyāma Śāstri's signature sound — the combination that appears in rāgas like Tōḍi, Bhairavī, and Ānandabhairavī, where the close proximity of R1 and G2 creates a cluster of Śrutis that the ear perceives as a single, complex, emotionally saturated region of tonal space.

Case Study: "Biranavārālaku" (Rāga Kalyāṇi, Melakarta 65)

This kṛti — one of Śyāma Śāstri's most famous — is an address to the Goddess Kāmākṣī in the rāga Kalyāṇi (Melakarta 65: Sa, R2, G3, M2, Pa, D2, N3).

Kalyāṇi is not typically a "weeping" rāga — it is bright, expansive, and auspicious. But Śyāma Śāstri uses it in a distinctive way: by emphasizing the Prati Madhyama (M2, Śruti 14), which adds a note of sharpness and urgency to the otherwise bright scale, and by placing his most emotionally intense Sanskrit syllables on the vulnerable notes (G3 and N3), he transforms Kalyāṇi from a rāga of celebration into a rāga of desperate, beautiful, urgent prayer.

The sāhitya: "Biranavārālaku — O Goddess, is there no one to protect me?" The word "biranavārālaku" (Telugu, with Sanskrit undertones) places the heavy syllable "bira" on a strong beat at a high pitch, creating a cry — a vocal gesture that is simultaneously musical, linguistic, and primal.

The healing mechanism is cathartic: the singer (and the listener who identifies with the singer) experiences the full force of the feeling of abandonment, vulnerability, and desperate need — and then, in the resolution of the musical phrase, experiences the relief of knowing that the Goddess is present, that the cry has been heard, that help is available. This cycle of distress → expression → relief → trust is the fundamental cycle of emotional healing, and Śyāma Śāstri's compositions facilitate it with extraordinary precision.

Chapter 2.8: Śaṅkarācārya's Saundaryalaharī and the 22 Śrutis as Waves of Beauty

Pages 88–92

The Saundaryalaharī: A Sonic Architecture

The title "Saundaryalaharī" means "Wave of Beauty" — and the metaphor of the wave (laharī) is itself profoundly musical. A wave is a periodic oscillation — a vibration — and the Sanskrit word "laharī" connotes the kind of undulating, rhythmic, aesthetically satisfying movement that characterizes both ocean waves and musical phrases.

Śaṅkara's text describes

continue

the Goddess's beauty as a series of waves — each verse a new crest, each image a new undulation of aesthetic pleasure. The 100 verses of the Saundaryalaharī can be understood as 100 Śrutis of beauty — 100 distinct microtonal inflections of the single, infinite beauty of the Goddess, each creating a slightly different aesthetic-emotional-spiritual effect, just as the 22 Śrutis create 22 distinct tonal effects within the single octave.

Verse 1: The Foundational Śruti

"śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum | na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api ||"

"If Śiva is united with Śakti, He becomes capable of creating. If not, He is not able even to stir."

This opening verse establishes the tonic — the fundamental relationship from which all subsequent beauty-waves will emerge. Just as Sa is the unchanging ground of the musical octave, the Śiva-Śakti unity is the unchanging ground of all creation and all beauty.

The word "spanditum" (to vibrate, to stir) is crucial. Śaṅkara identifies the fundamental creative act not as "making" or "constructing" but as vibrating — the same word used in the Tantric tradition for the primordial Nāda. Creation is vibration; beauty is vibration; the Goddess herself IS vibration — and without her vibration, even the absolute consciousness of Śiva remains motionless, silent, uncreative.

From the standpoint of the 22 Śrutis: this verse is Śruti 1 (Tīvrā) — the most fundamental, the most intense, the first pulse of the creative vibration. It establishes the ground upon which all subsequent Śrutis will be measured.

Verse 8: The Mūlādhāra Śruti

"sudhā-sindhor madhye sura-viṭapi-vāṭī-parivṛte | maṇi-dvīpe nīpopa-vanavati cintāmaṇi-gṛhe | śivākāre mañce paramaśiva-paryaṅka-nilayām | bhajanti tvāṃ dhanyāḥ katicana cidānanda-laharīm ||"

"In the middle of the ocean of nectar, in the island of jewels, in the grove of wish-fulfilling trees, in the house of the Cintāmaṇi gem, on the couch that is Śiva's form, a few blessed ones worship you, O Wave of Consciousness-Bliss."

This verse describes the innermost sanctum of the Śrī Cakra — the Bindu at the center, where the Goddess resides in her most intimate, most concentrated form. This is the Mūlādhāra Śruti — the fundamental vibration at the base of creation, the seed from which the entire tree of manifestation grows.

The phrase "cidānanda-laharīm" (O wave of consciousness-bliss) directly identifies the Goddess with a wave — a vibrational phenomenon. She is not a static form but a dynamic, oscillating, endlessly creative pulse — and the 22 Śrutis are 22 frequencies of this pulse, 22 modulations of her infinite beauty.

Dīkṣitar's Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa Kṛtis directly reference this verse and its imagery. His first āvaraṇa kṛti, in Rāga Ānandabhairavī, addresses the outermost enclosure of the Śrī Cakra and employs the soft, enveloping Śruti profile of Ānandabhairavī to create the sonic equivalent of the "ocean of nectar" described in the Saundaryalaharī. As the nine kṛtis progress inward toward the Bindu (the innermost enclosure), the rāgas become progressively more concentrated and more intense — mirroring the Saundaryalaharī's own journey from the periphery to the center of the Goddess's being.

Verses 42–100: The Goddess's Body as Śruti Map

The second half of the Saundaryalaharī describes the Goddess's beauty from head to toe, with each body part serving as a metaphor for a specific aspect of divine reality. From our perspective, each body part also corresponds to a specific region of the Śruti spectrum:

Chapter 2.9: Psychoacoustic Healing: How Microtones Affect the Nervous System

Pages 93–97

The Neuroscience of Microtonal Perception

Modern psychoacoustics — the science of how the brain perceives and processes sound — is beginning to provide empirical support for the therapeutic claims of the Rāga Cikitsā tradition.

Frequency and Neural Oscillation

The human brain operates through patterns of neural oscillation — rhythmic electrical activity that occurs at specific frequencies:

Brainwave Frequency Associated State
Delta 0.5–4 Hz Deep sleep, regeneration
Theta 4–8 Hz Meditation, creativity, memory
Alpha 8–13 Hz Relaxed alertness, calm
Beta 13–30 Hz Active thinking, focus
Gamma 30–100+ Hz Insight, peak awareness

When the ear receives a sustained musical tone, the auditory cortex responds with neural oscillations that are phase-locked to the frequency of the tone and its harmonics. This means that specific Śruti frequencies can entrain specific brainwave patterns:

  • Low Śrutis (those in the Sa and Re region, corresponding to lower absolute frequencies when Sa is set low) tend to entrain slower brainwave patterns → delta and theta → conducive to deep relaxation and healing

  • High Śrutis (those in the Dha and Ni region) tend to entrain faster brainwave patterns → alpha and beta → conducive to alertness and creative activity

The Difference Tone Phenomenon

When two tones are sounded simultaneously (as in a tānpurā drone), the brain perceives not only the two tones but also their difference tone — a phantom tone whose frequency equals the difference between the two sounded frequencies.

For example, if Sa is tuned to 240 Hz and Pa is tuned to 360 Hz, the difference tone is 360 – 240 = 120 Hz. This frequency falls in the range that the brain associates with active, focused awareness — suggesting that the traditional practice of singing with a Sa-Pa drone creates a neural environment conducive to concentration and meditation.

The 22 Śrutis, by specifying precise frequency ratios, determine the precise difference tones that will be generated — and therefore the precise brainwave entrainment effects that will occur. This is one of the mechanisms by which Śruti precision translates directly into therapeutic precision.

Vagal Stimulation Through Sound

The vagus nerve — the longest cranial nerve, running from the brainstem through the throat to the heart, lungs, and gut — plays a crucial role in the body's stress response and healing capacity.

The auricular branch of the vagus nerve innervates the outer ear — particularly the tragus and the cymba conchae. Sound waves entering the ear canal stimulate this branch, activating the vagus nerve and promoting parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) nervous system activity.

The specific frequencies and intervals of the 22 Śrutis, by creating specific patterns of vibration in the ear canal and tympanic membrane, stimulate the vagus nerve in specific ways:

  • Consonant intervals (Sa-Pa, Sa-Ma) produce smooth, regular vibration patterns → gentle vagal stimulation → relaxation

  • Moderately dissonant intervals (Sa-Ga, Sa-Dha) produce moderately complex vibration patterns → moderate vagal stimulation → emotional engagement

  • Strongly dissonant intervals (Sa-R1, Sa-N2) produce complex, irregular vibration patterns → strong vagal stimulation → arousal and catharsis

This vagal mechanism helps explain why Indian classical music — with its sustained drones, its precise intonation, and its microtonal ornamentations — has such powerful effects on the autonomic nervous system. Every Śruti is a specific vagal stimulus; every rāga is a specific vagal protocol.

The Pineal Gland and the Anusvāra

The anusvāra (Ṃ) — the nasal resonance that concludes every bījākṣara and many Sanskrit words — creates a sustained vibration in the nasal and cranial cavities. This vibration has been shown to:

  1. Increase nitric oxide production in the sinuses (by up to 15 times normal levels), promoting blood flow and immune function

  2. Stimulate the sphenoid sinus, which is located directly adjacent to the pituitary gland and the hypothalamus

  3. Create cranial resonance at frequencies that may stimulate the pineal gland — the gland associated with melatonin production, circadian rhythm regulation, and (in the yogic tradition) the Ājñā chakra

Dīkṣitar's compositions, rich in anusvāra-bearing Sanskrit words and bījākṣaras (OṂ, HRĪṂ, ŚRĪṂ, etc.), are thus vehicles for cranial resonance therapy — each anusvāra activating the nasal-cranial resonant cavity and stimulating the pineal-pituitary complex.

Śaṅkarācārya's verse compositions, when chanted aloud in the traditional manner (with sustained anusvāras and careful attention to nasalization), produce similar effects. The Saundaryalaharī in particular, with its dense Sanskrit and numerous nasal consonants, creates a sustained cranial resonance that may explain the text's traditional association with "opening the third eye" and enhancing spiritual vision.

The Polyvagal Theory and Rāga Therapy

Stephen Porges's Polyvagal Theory describes three neural circuits that govern the human stress response:

  1. Ventral vagal (social engagement): Active when we feel safe, connected, and engaged. Associated with eye contact, facial expression, prosodic (melodic) speech, and music.

  2. Sympathetic (fight-or-flight): Active when we feel threatened. Associated with increased heart rate, shallow breathing, and muscular tension.

  3. Dorsal vagal (shutdown): Active when we feel overwhelmed. Associated with immobilization, dissociation, and collapse.

Indian classical music, particularly the kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, operates primarily through the ventral vagal circuit — the circuit of safety, connection, and social engagement. The melodic contour of the rāga, the prosodic rhythm of the Sanskrit text, the warmth of the human voice — all of these are signals that activate the ventral vagal system, telling the listener's nervous system: "You are safe. You are held. You can relax and heal."

For patients whose nervous systems are stuck in sympathetic (anxiety, PTSD) or dorsal vagal (depression, dissociation) states, exposure to carefully selected rāgas and kṛtis can gradually shift the nervous system back toward ventral vagal dominance — restoring the capacity for connection, engagement, and healing.

This is the neurobiological basis for what the tradition has always known: that music heals, that Sanskrit heals, that devotion heals — and that the combination of music, Sanskrit, and devotion heals at every level of the human being.

Principles of Śruti Prescription

Based on this pharmacopoeia, we can formulate general principles for Śruti-based therapeutic prescription:

1. For Vāta Disorders (anxiety, insomnia, irregular rhythms, dryness, pain):

  • Emphasize the Sa and Pa Śrutis (grounding, stabilizing)

  • Use Chandovatī (Śruti 4, rhythmic ordering) and Mandā (Śruti 3, gentle sedation)

  • Avoid excessive use of Kṣobhiṇī (Śruti 22, agitating) and Raudrī (Śruti 8, cathartic)

2. For Pitta Disorders (inflammation, anger, heartburn, skin conditions):

  • Emphasize the cooling Śrutis: Kumudvatī (2), Dayāvatī (5), Ramyā (20)

  • Use the sweet intervals: Ranjanī (6), Madantī (18)

  • Avoid Krodhā (9, energizing) and Sandīpanī (16, fire-kindling)

3. For Kapha Disorders (lethargy, congestion, depression, weight gain):

  • Emphasize the stimulating Śrutis: Krodhā (9), Sandīpanī (16), Ugrā (21), Kṣobhiṇī (22)

  • Use the energizing intervals: Raudrī (8), Raktā (15)

  • Avoid excessive Mandā (3, sedating) and Kumudvatī (2, cooling)

These principles guide the selection of Melakartas and specific compositions for therapeutic use — the subject of Section III.

Section III: The 72 Melakarta Rāgas — The Complete Melodic Healing System · II

❖

Pages 101–150

Chapter 3.1: The Architecture of 72: Pūrvāṅga, Uttarāṅga, and Structural Logic

Pages 101–106

The Two Halves of the Scale

Every Melakarta Rāga is composed of two halves:

Pūrvāṅga (the lower tetrachord): Sa – Re – Ga – Ma This half establishes the foundation of the rāga — its basic character, its primary emotional color, its grounding quality. The Pūrvāṅga is like the trunk of a tree — stable, rooted, providing structure.

Uttarāṅga (the upper tetrachord): Pa – Dha – Ni – Sa (upper) This half establishes the aspiration of the rāga — its emotional reach, its spiritual direction, its movement toward transcendence. The Uttarāṅga is like the branches and leaves of the tree — reaching upward, responding to light, expressing the tree's highest potential.

The therapeutic character of a Melakarta is determined by the interaction of these two halves:

  • A stable Pūrvāṅga (with consonant intervals between Sa-Re-Ga-Ma) combined with a stable Uttarāṅga (with consonant intervals between Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa) creates a rāga of comprehensive stability — suitable for grounding, calming, and centering. Example: Melakarta 29, Śaṅkarābharaṇam (Dhīraśaṅkarābharaṇam).

  • A tense Pūrvāṅga (with dissonant intervals) combined with a tense Uttarāṅga creates a rāga of comprehensive intensity — suitable for catharsis, confrontation, and dramatic transformation. Example: Melakarta 8, Hanumatōḍi.

  • A stable Pūrvāṅga with a tense Uttarāṅga creates a rāga that is grounded but aspiring — rooted in the earth but reaching toward the sky. Example: Melakarta 15, Māyāmāḷavagauḷa.

  • A tense Pūrvāṅga with a stable Uttarāṅga creates a rāga that is challenging at the base but resolving in the heights — a rāga of struggle followed by release. Example: Melakarta 51, Kāmavardhini.

The 12 Chakra Groups: A Therapeutic Typology

The 12 Chakra groups of the Melakarta system correspond to 12 fundamental therapeutic modalities:

Chakra Name Melakartas Pūrvāṅga Character Therapeutic Modality
I Indu (Moon) 1–6 R1-G1-M1: Minimal, sparse Deep rest, silence, withdrawal
II Netra (Eye) 7–12 R1-G2-M1: Gentle opening Gentle vision, soft awakening
III Agni (Fire) 13–18 R1-G3-M1: Bright emergence Illumination, clarity, insight
IV Veda (Knowledge) 19–24 R2-G2-M1: Balanced center Wisdom, learning, understanding
V Bāṇa (Arrow) 25–30 R2-G3-M1: Directed energy Focused action, determination
VI Ṛtu (Season) 31–36 R3-G3-M1: Full expression Natural rhythm, seasonal flow
VII Ṛṣi (Sage) 37–42 R1-G1-M2: Altered foundation Altered consciousness, insight
VIII Vasu (Wealth) 43–48 R1-G2-M2: Generous expansion Abundance, generosity, flow
IX Brahma (Creator) 49–54 R1-G3-M2: Creative explosion Creativity, innovation, birth
X Diśi (Direction) 55–60 R2-G2-M2: Spatial awareness Orientation, navigation, clarity
XI Rudra (Storm) 61–66 R2-G3-M2: Fierce transformation Catharsis, destruction of patterns
XII Āditya (Sun) 67–72 R3-G3-M2: Maximum intensity Solar power, ultimate transcendence

The Healing Logic

The progression from Chakra I to Chakra XII traces a therapeutic arc:

Chakras I–III (Melakartas 1–18): The quieting phase — progressive emergence from silence and rest. Appropriate for the beginning of a healing process, when the patient needs to move from agitation to calm, from chaos to order.

Chakras IV–VI (Melakartas 19–36): The balancing phase — the establishment of equilibrium and natural rhythm. Appropriate for the middle of a healing process, when the patient needs to consolidate gains and establish stable patterns.

Chakras VII–IX (Melakartas 37–54): The transforming phase — the introduction of altered states and creative possibilities through the Prati Madhyama. Appropriate for the breakthrough phase of healing, when deep-seated patterns need to be challenged and transformed.

Chakras X–XII (Melakartas 55–72): The transcending phase — maximum intensity and ultimate resolution. Appropriate for the completion of a healing process, when the patient is ready for the most profound transformation — the recognition of their true nature as infinite consciousness.

This 12-stage therapeutic arc mirrors:

  • The 12 months of the year (healing follows natural rhythms)

  • The 12 rāśis (zodiac signs) of Jyotiṣa (healing follows cosmic rhythms)

  • The 12 ādityas (solar deities) of Vedic mythology (healing follows the sun's journey)

  • The 12 petals of the Anāhata chakra (healing originates in the heart)

Chapter 3.2: Melakartas 1–12 (Chakras I–II): The Foundation Rāgas

Pages 107–112

Chakra I: Indu (Moon) — Melakartas 1–6

The first six Melakartas share the Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G1 – M1

This is the sparsest, most minimal Pūrvāṅga — both Re and Ga are at their lowest positions, creating the narrowest possible interval cluster in the lower tetrachord. The three notes R1, G1, and M1 are close together, almost touching — creating a quality of intimacy, interiority, and quiet intensity.

Therapeutically, these rāgas are sedative and introspective — they draw the listener inward, away from the stimulation of the external world, into a quiet inner space where healing can occur undisturbed.

Melakarta 1: Kanakaṅgi — Sa R1 G1 M1 Pa D1 N1 Sa

The most "closed" of all Melakartas — both halves are at their minimum. This rāga creates an extremely introverted, enclosed, protected sonic space. Therapeutically, it is prescribed for:

  • Severe anxiety with hypervigilance (creates a sense of safe enclosure)

  • Overstimulation (withdraws attention from external stimuli)

  • Insomnia due to nervous agitation

Dīkṣitar composed no kṛtis in this rāga (nor did Śyāma Śāstri), reflecting its extreme rarity in performance. However, the theoretical existence of Kanakaṅgi within the system is therapeutically significant — it represents the possibility of absolute withdrawal, the deepest possible rest.

In Śaṅkarācārya's framework, Kanakaṅgi corresponds to the state described in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad as Suṣupti (deep sleep) — the state in which all external awareness ceases and the individual rests in the causal body. Śaṅkara writes in the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi:

"suṣuptau manaso nāśaḥ na tu tattvasya naśyati" "In deep sleep, the mind dissolves, but the Self does not perish."

Kanakaṅgi is the musical equivalent of this statement — in its extreme interiority, the mind's habitual patterns are suspended, but the Self remains, healing silently in the background.

Melakarta 3: Gānamurti — Sa R1 G1 M1 Pa D1 N3 Sa

The introduction of N3 (Kākali Niṣāda, Śruti 22, Kṣobhiṇī) in the Uttarāṅga creates a striking contrast — the extremely closed lower half opens suddenly in the upper half, like a window opening in a sealed room. This "window of transcendence" in an otherwise introverted rāga is therapeutically powerful for:

  • Depression with withdrawal (the N3 provides a ray of hope)

  • Agoraphobia (the gradual opening from enclosure to spaciousness)

  • Grief that has become stuck (the N3 provides a channel for upward release)

Melakarta 5: Manōrañjani — Sa R1 G1 M1 Pa D2 N2 Sa

The name means "mind-delighting" — and the introduction of D2 (Catusśruti Dhaivata) and N2 (Kaiśiki Niṣāda) in the Uttarāṅga creates a warmer, more emotionally accessible upper half. This rāga combines introversion in the lower tetrachord with warmth in the upper — therapeutically useful for:

  • Social anxiety (introversion that is held, not isolating)

  • Mild depression (the warmth of D2 and N2 lifts the mood without overstimulating)

Chakra II: Netra (Eye) — Melakartas 7–12

The second six Melakartas share the Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G2 – M1

The shift from G1 to G2 (Sādhāraṇa Gāndhāra) opens the lower tetrachord slightly — the interval between Ga and Ma widens, creating more emotional space and a quality of gentle awakening, like eyes slowly opening.

Melakarta 8: Hanumatōḍi — Sa R1 G2 M1 Pa D1 N2 Sa

This is one of the most important rāgas in the entire Carnatic system — the basis of the famous Rāga Tōḍi (Śuddha Tōḍi) and its numerous janya rāgas. Its Śruti profile is:

  • R1 (Dayāvatī — compassion)

  • G2 (Raudrī — emotional release)

  • D1 (Madantī — intoxication)

  • N2 (Ugrā — power)

This combination creates a rāga of profound emotional depth — tender, vulnerable, poignant, yet possessed of great inner strength. It is the rāga of Karuṇa Rasa — the aesthetic emotion of compassion.

Dīkṣitar's kṛti in Tōḍi: Several exist, including "Guruguha tāraṃ" — "Guruguha, the deliverer." The sāhitya invokes Muruga/Subrahmaṇya as the guru who delivers from suffering. The combination of Tōḍi's deep emotional quality with the invocation of the divine deliverer creates a complete therapeutic intervention for grief and loss — the rāga opens the wound, the sāhitya provides the medicine.

Śyāma Śāstri's kṛtis in Tōḍi: Several masterpieces, including "Dēvī brōva samayamidē" — "O Goddess, this is the time to protect me!" The desperate urgency of the text, carried by Tōḍi's depth, creates the emotional equivalent of a dam breaking — decades of suppressed pain, fear, and longing pour out in a torrent of musical catharsis. The therapeutic effect is profound: the singer (and the fully engaged listener) emerges from this experience lighter, cleaner, more spacious — the emotional toxins have been released, and the natural healing capacity of the heart has been restored.

Śaṅkarācārya connection: The Karuṇa quality of Tōḍi corresponds to the quality Śaṅkara calls "Dayā" (compassion) — which he identifies, in the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, as one of the essential qualities of the spiritual aspirant:

"ahiṃsā satya-astēyaṃ brahmacaryam aparigrahaḥ | dayā kṣāntiś ca sarva-ēṣu sāmānyāni samāhitāḥ ||"

"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possessiveness, compassion, and patience toward all — these are the universal virtues."

Tōḍi is the rāga of dayā — the rāga that opens the heart to compassion, first for oneself (through cathartic emotional release) and then for all beings (through the expanded awareness that follows catharsis). This is healing at the deepest level — not merely the cure of a specific disease but the cultivation of a fundamental virtue that transforms the entire quality of life.

Melakarta 12: Rūpāvati — Sa R1 G2 M1 Pa D3 N3 Sa

The most "open" rāga of Chakra II — with D3 and N3 in the upper tetrachord creating a bright, expansive quality. Therapeutically, this rāga represents the completion of the gentle awakening process initiated by Chakra I — the eyes are now fully open, the light is streaming in, the healing vision is clear.

Chapter 3.3: Melakartas 13–24 (Chakras III–IV): The Middle Rāgas

Pages 113–118

Chakra III: Agni (Fire) — Melakartas 13–18

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G3 – M1

The introduction of G3 (Antara Gāndhāra — the bright, high major third) creates a luminous, radiant quality in the lower tetrachord. The wide interval from R1 to G3 is a leap of light — a burst of solar energy that transforms the introverted quality of Chakras I and II into something bright, warm, and expansive.

This is the Agni (fire) group — the rāgas of illumination, purification, and transformative heat.

Melakarta 15: Māyāmāḷavagauḷa — Sa R1 G3 M1 Pa D1 N3 Sa

This is arguably the most important Melakarta in Carnatic music pedagogy — it is the first scale taught to beginners, and it appears in countless compositions. Its structure combines:

  • R1 and D1 (low, gentle) with G3 and N3 (high, bright) — creating a zigzag pattern of low-high-low-high that alternates between shadow and light, tension and release, descent and ascent.

This zigzag pattern is inherently balancing — it prevents the listener from getting stuck in either extreme (too dark or too bright) and keeps the consciousness in a state of dynamic equilibrium. Therapeutically, Māyāmāḷavagauḷa is prescribed for:

  • General balancing (tri-doṣa conditions)

  • Mood regulation (neither manic nor depressive)

  • Cognitive flexibility (the alternation between low and high exercises the brain's capacity to shift between states)

Dīkṣitar's kṛtis in Māyāmāḷavagauḷa: Many important compositions, including "Mēdini lōka" and "Mahāgaṇapatim". The latter — "The Great Gaṇapati" — is one of the most frequently performed Dīkṣitar kṛtis and is traditionally sung at the beginning of concerts to remove obstacles (Gaṇapati/Gaṇeśa being the remover of obstacles).

The therapeutic intention is clear: Māyāmāḷavagauḷa, with its balanced, obstacle-dissolving quality, combined with the invocation of Gaṇeśa (the deity who removes both physical and psychological obstacles), creates a powerful clearing intervention — removing the blockages that prevent the natural flow of health, energy, and creativity.

The Sanskrit sāhitya "Mahāgaṇapatim manasā smarāmi" means "I meditate in my mind on the Great Gaṇapati." The word "manasā" (in the mind) is significant — the healing is directed specifically at the mental level (Manomaya Kośa), addressing the mental obstacles (fear, doubt, confusion, rigidity) that obstruct healing at every other level.

Śaṅkarācārya connection: Śaṅkara's own invocation to Gaṇeśa — the celebrated "Mudākarātta Mōdakaṃ" — shares the same therapeutic intent:

"mudā-karātta mōdakaṃ sadā vimukti sādhakaṃ | kalā-dharāvatam-sakaṃ vilāsi lōka rakṣakaṃ ||"

"He who joyfully holds the sweet modaka, who is ever the means to liberation, who bears the crescent moon, who playfully protects the world..."

The combination of joy (mudā), sweetness (modaka), liberation (vimukti), and protection (rakṣa) in this verse creates the same therapeutic profile as Māyāmāḷavagauḷa — balanced, clearing, gently joyful, and protective.

Chakra IV: Veda (Knowledge) — Melakartas 19–24

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R2 – G2 – M1

The introduction of R2 (Catusśruti Ṛṣabha — the moderately bright second) creates a warm, wise, centered quality. R2 and G2 are equidistant from Sa and Ma, creating a sense of symmetry and balance in the lower tetrachord.

This is the Veda group — the rāgas of knowledge, learning, and understanding. These rāgas neither sedate nor stimulate; they illuminate — they create the mental conditions conducive to clear thinking, deep comprehension, and wise discernment.

Melakarta 22: Kharaharapriyā — Sa R2 G2 M1 Pa D2 N2 Sa

One of the most beloved and most performed Melakartas — the basis of the enormously important janya Rāga Kāmbhōji, Sahāna, Śrīrañjani, and many others.

Its Śruti profile:

  • R2 (Rati — pleasure)

  • G2 (Raudrī — emotional release)

  • D2 (Rohiṇī — growth)

  • N2 (Ugrā — power)

This combination creates a rāga of moderate emotional depth — not as intense as Tōḍi (Melakarta 8) but more emotionally engaging than Śaṅkarābharaṇam (Melakarta 29). It is the "Goldilocks rāga" — not too dark, not too bright, just right.

Dīkṣitar's kṛtis in Kharaharapriyā and its janyas: Many significant compositions. In Kāmbhōji, Dīkṣitar composed the magnificent "Śrī Subrahmaṇyāya Namaste" (discussed in Chapter 1.4). In the parent Kharaharapriyā itself, compositions like "Śrī Rājagopālam" demonstrate the rāga's capacity for warm, devotional expression.

Śyāma Śāstri's kṛtis in rāgas derived from Kharaharapriyā are among his finest. In Sāhana (a janya), his "Ō Jagadambā nanu brōvu" — "O Mother of the Universe, will you not protect me?" — exemplifies the rāga's capacity for tender, intimate emotional expression.

Melakarta 20: Naṭabhairavī — Sa R2 G2 M1 Pa D1 N2 Sa

The basis of the supremely important janya Ānandabhairavī — the rāga Śyāma Śāstri most frequently chose for his compositions. Naṭabhairavī combines the warmth of R2-G2 with the depth of D1-N2, creating a quality of warm depth — emotionally accessible but profound.

Dīkṣitar's Kāmalāmbā Navāvaraṇa cycle begins with a kṛti in Ānandabhairavī, confirming this rāga's role as the gateway to the deepest healing — the first enclosure of the Śrī Cakra, the first step on the journey toward the Bindu.

Chapter 3.4: Melakartas 25–36 (Chakras V–VI): The Expansive Rāgas

Pages 119–124

Chakra V: Bāṇa (Arrow) — Melakartas 25–30

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R2 – G3 – M1

The combination of R2 with G3 creates a wide, bright, directed interval — the second and third are well-separated, creating a sense of spaciousness and direction. These are the rāgas of focused action — the arrow flying toward its target.

Melakarta 28: Harikāmbhōji — Sa R2 G3 M1 Pa D2 N2 Sa

The basis of numerous important janyas including Kāmbhōji, Kēdāragauḷa, Surāṭi, and others. This Melakarta combines brightness (R2-G3) with warmth (D2-N2), creating one of the most universally appealing tonal profiles in Indian music.

The name "Harikāmbhōji" contains the word Hari (Viṣṇu) — and the rāga indeed has a Vaiṣṇava quality: warm, nurturing, protective, sustaining. Therapeutically, it is prescribed for:

  • General well-being and health maintenance

  • Convalescence (the warm, nurturing quality supports recovery)

  • Pitta conditions (the warmth is nourishing, not overheating)

Melakarta 29: Dhīraśaṅkarābharaṇam — Sa R2 G3 M1 Pa D2 N3 Sa

The "Jewel of Śaṅkara" — the Indian major scale. As discussed in Chapter 2.6, this rāga is the broadest-spectrum therapeutic agent in the Melakarta system.

Dīkṣitar composed extensively in Śaṅkarābharaṇam and its janyas. His "Akṣayaliṅga Vibho" (analyzed in Chapter 2.6) is a comprehensive healing composition.

Śaṅkarācārya connection: The rāga's name literally means "the ornament (ābharaṇam) of Śaṅkara (Śiva/Śaṅkarācārya)" — and it is indeed the rāga that most fully embodies Śaṅkara's philosophical vision of Brahman as sat-cit-ānanda (being-consciousness-bliss):

  • Sat (being) is expressed by the stable, grounded Sa-Pa framework

  • Cit (consciousness) is expressed by the bright, clear R2-G3 and D2-N3 intervals

  • Ānanda (bliss) is expressed by the overall quality of balance, harmony, and beauty

Chakra VI: Ṛtu (Season) — Melakartas 31–36

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R3 – G3 – M1

Both R3 and G3 are at their highest positions — creating the widest possible separation between Sa and Re, and a very close relationship between Re and Ga (since R3 is enharmonically equivalent to G2). This creates a unique quality: a wide, open beginning (the large Sa-Re gap) followed by a close, intimate middle (the narrow Re-Ga proximity).

These are the seasonal rāgas — rāgas that embody the quality of natural, cyclical change. Therapeutically, they address conditions related to seasonal transitions, circadian rhythm disorders, and the need for adaptive flexibility.

Melakarta 36: Calanāṭa — Sa R3 G3 M1 Pa D3 N3 Sa

The most "open" of all the Śuddha Madhyama Melakartas — every variable svara is at its highest position. This creates a rāga of maximum brightness and expansion — all intervals are wide, all spaces are open, the entire tonal field radiates outward.

Therapeutically, Calanāṭa is prescribed for:

  • Kapha conditions (the wide, bright intervals dissolve stagnation and heaviness)

  • Winter lethargy (the solar quality counteracts the seasonal tendency toward withdrawal)

  • Creative blocks (the maximum openness stimulates imagination and innovation)

Chapter 3.5: Melakartas 37–48 (Chakras VII–VIII): The Prati Madhyama Foundation

Pages 125–130

The Significance of Prati Madhyama

Melakartas 37–72 all employ Prati Madhyama (M2) — the raised fourth degree. This single change — raising Ma by one Śruti — transforms the entire character of the scale:

  1. The interval between Ga and Ma narrows. Where Śuddha Ma is a full fourth above Sa, Prati Ma is an augmented fourth — creating a sense of heightened tension and aspiration in the lower tetrachord.

  2. The interval between Ma and Pa narrows. The augmented fourth to the fifth is a smaller interval than the natural fourth to the fifth — creating a compression in the upper part of the lower tetrachord that gives a quality of urgency and intensity.

  3. The tritone relationship between Sa and M2 (the "devil's interval" of Western music theory) creates a fundamental instability that can be either unsettling or electrifying, depending on the context and the performer's mastery.

Therapeutically, the Prati Madhyama Melakartas are the transformative agents of the system — they introduce disruption, instability, and altered states that are necessary for deep healing. Just as a fever is the body's way of fighting infection, the Prati Madhyama's "fever pitch" is the musical system's way of fighting stagnation, complacency, and resistance to change.

Chakra VII: Ṛṣi (Sage) — Melakartas 37–42

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G1 – M2

The combination of the most closed Re-Ga pair (R1-G1) with the raised Ma creates an extraordinary tension — the lower tetrachord is simultaneously compressed (R1-G1 cluster) and stretched (the wide G1-to-M2 gap). This creates a quality of visionary intensity — the sage's state of consciousness, in which ordinary reality is compressed and transcendent reality is stretched open.

Melakarta 39: Jhālavarāḷi — Sa R1 G1 M2 Pa D1 N2 Sa

One of the most dramatic rāgas in the system — the combination of the tight R1-G1-M2 cluster with the somber D1-N2 creates a rāga of extreme intensity and emotional depth. In the Rāga Cikitsā tradition, Jhālavarāḷi is prescribed for:

  • Severe depression (not the gentle sadness of Tōḍi, but the profound darkness that requires equally profound confrontation)

  • Psychospiritual crisis (the "dark night of the soul")

  • Conditions requiring maximum transformation (entrenched addictions, chronic self-destructive patterns)

The rāga's extreme quality makes it unsuitable for casual therapeutic use — it is the musical equivalent of a powerful, potentially toxic medicine that must be administered with great skill and care.

Chakra VIII: Vasu (Wealth) — Melakartas 43–48

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G2 – M2

The introduction of G2 softens the intensity of Chakra VII — the lower tetrachord now has a gentle opening (G2 is wider than G1) combined with the Prati Madhyama's aspiring quality. These rāgas are generous and abundant — the Vasus (deities of wealth and prosperity) expressed in sound.

Melakarta 44: Bhāvapriyā — Sa R1 G2 M2 Pa D1 N3 Sa

The name means "beloved of feeling" — and indeed, this rāga, with its combination of G2's emotional warmth and M2's aspiring quality, creates a sonic space in which deep feeling can arise naturally and safely. Therapeutically:

  • Emotional numbness (the warm-yet-intense quality thaws frozen feelings)

  • Post-traumatic states (the safe spaciousness of the Uttarāṅga provides containment for the intensity of the Pūrvāṅga's emotional activation)

Chapter 3.6: Melakartas 49–60 (Chakras IX–X): The Prati Madhyama Middle

Pages 131–136

Chakra IX: Brahma (Creator) — Melakartas 49–54

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R1 – G3 – M2

The combination of G3 (the bright, high major third) with M2 (the raised fourth) creates the most expansive and creative Pūrvāṅga in the system. The wide intervals Sa-R1 (small) and R1-G3 (very large) create a pattern of contraction followed by explosion — the seed bursting open, the creative impulse breaking through.

Melakarta 51: Kāmavardhini (Pantuvarāḷi) — Sa R1 G3 M2 Pa D1 N3 Sa

One of the most powerful and majestic rāgas in the Carnatic system. The combination of R1 (low, compressed) with G3 (high, bright) and M2 (raised, aspiring) creates a lower tetrachord of extraordinary drama — a journey from the depths to the heights in the space of four notes.

The addition of D1 (low, dark) and N3 (high, bright) in the upper tetrachord mirrors this journey, creating a double arc — descent and ascent in both halves of the scale.

Dīkṣitar's kṛtis in Pantuvarāḷi: The magnificent "Ratnādhiṣṭhitam" — describing the deity as "seated upon jewels." The sāhitya's imagery of radiant gemstones mirrors the rāga's own jewel-like quality — each note a facet, each interval a flash of light.

Therapeutically, Kāmavardhini is prescribed for:

  • Conditions requiring dramatic transformation (the rāga's extreme intervallic contrasts shake loose entrenched patterns)

  • Spiritual stagnation (the rāga's majestic quality evokes the grandeur of the Self, awakening the practitioner from the small, constricted ego-identity)

  • Low self-esteem and lack of confidence (the rāga's nobility and power transfer to the listener, evoking the feeling of inner royalty)

Śaṅkarācārya connection: Kāmavardhini's quality of dramatic transformation corresponds to Śaṅkara's teaching on Vairāgya (dispassion) — the radical letting go of attachment that is the prerequisite for liberation:

"vairāgyam ca mumukṣutvaṃ tīvraṃ yasya tu vidyate | tasminn evārtha-vān eṣa phala-vān eva lakṣaṇaḥ ||" (Vivekacūḍāmaṇi)

"In whom intense dispassion and intense desire for liberation exist — for that one alone is this teaching fruitful."

The intensity that Śaṅkara demands (tīvraṃ — "fierce, intense") is precisely the quality that Kāmavardhini embodies. This is not gentle music for gentle people; it is fierce music for those ready for fierce transformation.

Chakra X: Diśi (Direction) — Melakartas 55–60

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R2 – G2 – M2

The balanced, centered quality of R2-G2 combined with the aspiring quality of M2 creates rāgas of oriented expansion — spacious but not directionless, ambitious but not reckless.

Melakarta 57: Simhendramadhyamam — Sa R2 G2 M2 Pa D1 N3 Sa

A rāga of extraordinary spatial quality — the wide intervals in the Uttarāṅga (D1 to N3 is an enormous leap) create a sense of vast, open space — like standing on a mountaintop and seeing the horizon in every direction.

This rāga is the basis for some profoundly healing compositions. Dīkṣitar's "Dākṣiṇya Suraviṇōdhini" in this rāga demonstrates how the spatial quality can be used to expand the listener's sense of self beyond the confines of the body and mind.

Chapter 3.7: Melakartas 61–72 (Chakras XI–XII): The Prati Madhyama Completion

Pages 137–141

Chakra XI: Rudra (Storm) — Melakartas 61–66

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R2 – G3 – M2

The bright G3 combined with the raised M2 creates the maximum tension in the lower tetrachord — the Rudra (fierce Śiva) energy, the thunderstorm that clears the air, the lightning bolt that illuminates by destroying darkness.

Melakarta 65: Mecakalyāṇi (Kalyāṇi) — Sa R2 G3 M2 Pa D2 N3 Sa

The "Queen of Rāgas" — the most beloved and most performed of all Prati Madhyama Melakartas. Kalyāṇi combines the brightness of G3-M2 with the warmth of D2-N3, creating a rāga of radiant beauty — solar, expansive, auspicious.

The name "Kalyāṇi" means "auspicious, beautiful, bestowing welfare" — and the rāga lives up to its name at every level:

  • Physical: The wide, bright intervals stimulate circulation, digestion, and respiratory function

  • Emotional: The warm, expansive quality dissolves depression, anxiety, and emotional constriction

  • Spiritual: The solar quality evokes the experience of inner light, Self-recognition, and freedom

Dīkṣitar's kṛtis in Kalyāṇi: Multiple masterpieces, including the sublime "Ēhi Annapūrṇe" — "Come, O Annapūrṇā (Goddess of Nourishment)!" The Goddess Annapūrṇā is invoked as the provider of both physical food and spiritual sustenance — and Kalyāṇi, with its warm brightness, is the perfect sonic vehicle for this invocation.

The sāhitya's opening word "Ēhi" (Come!) is a direct imperative — not a passive prayer but an active summons, a command born of devotion so intense that it becomes confident rather than submissive. This is the voice of the child calling to the Mother with perfect trust — "Come! I know you will come, because you are my Mother and you love me."

Śyāma Śāstri's kṛti in Kalyāṇi: "Biranavārālaku" — analyzed in Chapter 2.7. Where Dīkṣitar uses Kalyāṇi for confident, solar invocation, Śyāma Śāstri uses it for desperate, vulnerable prayer — demonstrating the rāga's extraordinary therapeutic range: it can heal the confident and the vulnerable alike, the strong and the weak, the solar and the lunar.

Śaṅkarācārya connection: Kalyāṇi's auspicious quality corresponds directly to Śaṅkara's concept of Maṅgala — the supreme auspiciousness that characterizes Brahman:

"maṅgalaṃ bhagavān viṣṇur maṅgalaṃ garuḍa-dhvajaḥ | maṅgalaṃ puṇḍarīkākṣo maṅgalāyatano hariḥ ||"

This verse (attributed to Śaṅkara in some traditions) identifies Viṣṇu with maṅgala (auspiciousness) — the same auspiciousness that Kalyāṇi embodies in sound. To listen to Kalyāṇi with full attention is to receive the Maṅgala of Brahman through the ear — to be bathed in auspiciousness, to be healed by beauty.

Chakra XII: Āditya (Sun) — Melakartas 67–72

Pūrvāṅga: Sa – R3 – G3 – M2

The maximum Pūrvāṅga — both Re and Ga at their highest positions, combined with the raised Ma. This creates the most intensely bright, maximally expansive lower tetrachord — the full power of the Sun (Āditya) concentrated in four notes.

Melakarta 72: Rasikapriyā — Sa R3 G3 M2 Pa D3 N3 Sa

The final Melakarta — the culmination of the entire system. Every variable svara is at its maximum position; the scale is as wide, as bright, as open as possible. This is the rāga of complete transcendence — the moment when all limitation has been dissolved, all darkness has been illuminated, all contraction has been expanded.

The name "Rasikapriyā" means "beloved of the connoisseur" — and indeed, this rāga requires the most refined musical sensibility to appreciate and to perform. It is the musical equivalent of the Mahāvākya "Tat Tvam Asi" (That Thou Art) — the supreme statement of non-duality, in which all distinction between self and Absolute, between individual and universal, between listener and sound, is dissolved.

Therapeutically, Rasikapriyā is prescribed for:

  • The final stage of a healing process (when all that remains is the recognition of wholeness)

  • Existential crisis (when the only cure is the recognition that the Self was never sick)

  • Preparation for death (when the body is released and consciousness returns to its infinite source)

Śyāma Śāstri's Rāga Palette

Unlike Dīkṣitar, who ranged widely across the Melakarta system, Śyāma Śāstri concentrated on a relatively small number of rāgas — choosing them not for their theoretical interest but for their emotional healing potential:

Rāga Parent Melakarta No. of Kṛtis (approx.) Emotional-Therapeutic Quality

The concentration on a few rāgas is itself therapeutically significant. Śyāma Śāstri was not interested in demonstrating his knowledge of the entire system; he was interested in going as deep as possible into the healing potential of each rāga. By composing multiple kṛtis in the same rāga, he explored different facets of its therapeutic personality — different angles of approach, different emotional depths, different stages of the healing journey.

This approach mirrors the clinical practice of prescribing the same medicine in different dosages and combinations to address different stages and aspects of the same condition. Ānandabhairavī is Śyāma Śāstri's "medicine of choice" — and his multiple kṛtis in this rāga constitute different preparations of the same fundamental therapeutic substance.

Chapter 3.10: The 72 Melakartas as a Map of Human Consciousness

Pages 149–150

The 72 Melakarta system, fully understood, is not merely a classification of scales. It is a map of all possible states of human consciousness — 72 distinct modes of experiencing reality, 72 distinct relationships between the individual and the infinite, 72 distinct healing pathways from suffering to wholeness.

Each Melakarta embodies a specific combination of:

  • Grounding (Sa-Pa stability)

  • Emotional quality (Re-Ga-Ma relationship)

  • Aspiration (Dha-Ni-Sa relationship)

  • Tension/resolution (M1 vs. M2)

These four parameters, in their 72 possible combinations, cover the complete range of human psychological possibility — from the deepest withdrawal (Melakarta 1) to the most radiant transcendence (Melakarta 72), from the gentlest tenderness (Melakartas in Chakra II) to the fiercest transformation (Melakartas in Chakra XI).

The kṛtis of Dīkṣitar and Śyāma Śāstri, set within this system and enriched by their Sanskrit sāhitya and their devotional intentionality, are guided tours of this map — carefully designed journeys through specific regions of consciousness, conducted by master guides who know every path, every danger, and every refuge.

And Śaṅkarācārya's philosophical literature provides the legend of the map — the explanation of what the territories mean, why they exist, and what lies beyond them all.

Chapter 4.1: Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar: Biography, Lineage, and Spiritual Vision

Pages 151–155

Early Life and Formation

Muttuswāmi Dīkṣitar was born in 1775 in Tiruvārūr, a temple town in the Tanjore (Thanjavur) district of Tamil Nadu, into a family of Smārta Brahmins deeply engaged in both Vedic learning and musical practice. His father, Rāmaswāmi Dīkṣitar, was himself a distinguished musician and composer — one of the pioneers who integrated Western harmonic elements into Carnatic music through the composition of Nōṭṭusvara Sāhityas (Sanskrit texts set to Western-influenced melodies).

The young Muttuswāmi received a comprehensive education that encompassed:

  1. Vedic learning: Sanskrit grammar (Vyākaraṇa), Vedic chanting, and the study of the Upaniṣads and Śāstras

  2. Musical training: From his father, in the traditions of Carnatic Saṅgīta

  3. Mantra Śāstra: The science of sacred formulae, including the Śrī Vidyā system of goddess worship

  4. Jyotiṣa: Vedic astrology, which would later inform his Navagraha Kṛtis

A pivotal event in Dīkṣitar's spiritual formation was his encounter with the ascetic Cidambranātha Yogi at Vārāṇasī (Benaras), during a journey undertaken in his youth. Under Cidambranātha's guidance, Dīkṣitar was initiated into:

  • Śrī Vidyā Upāsanā: The worship of the Goddess through the Śrī Cakra (the supreme sacred diagram of Hindu Tantra)

  • Kuṇḍalinī Yoga: The practice of awakening the serpent energy at the base of the spine and guiding it through the chakras to the crown

  • Mantra Dīkṣā: Initiation into specific mantras, including the supreme Pañcadaśī and Ṣoḍaśī mantras of Śrī Vidyā

This initiation transformed Dīkṣitar from a talented musician into a mantravādin — a wielder of sacred sound. From this point forward, his compositions were not merely musical works but mantra-structures — carefully designed sonic architectures intended to activate the specific energies of the ��rī Cakra within the singer and the listener.

The Signature: Guruguha

Dīkṣitar incorporated the word "Guruguha" into virtually every one of his compositions — a practice known as mudrā (signature or seal). "Guruguha" is a name of Lord Subrahmaṇya (Muruga, Kārttikeya) — the son of Śiva and Pārvatī, the god of war, wisdom, and the planet Mars. But "Guruguha" also means "the guru who dwells in the cave (of the heart)" — identifying the deity with the inner teacher, the Ātman, the Self that is discovered in the cave of meditation.

By embedding "Guruguha" in every composition, Dīkṣitar accomplished several therapeutic functions simultaneously:

  1. Mantra repetition: Every time the kṛti is performed, the name "Guruguha" is chanted — functioning as a mantra that invokes the divine presence

  2. Self-remembrance: The name reminds the performer and listener that the true guru is within — that healing ultimately comes from the Self, not from any external source

  3. Sonic signature: The specific phonemes of "Guruguha" (Gu-ru-gu-ha: guttural + retroflex + guttural + aspirate) create a specific pattern of articulatory activation that stimulates the throat, palate, and cranium

The Compositional Method: Mantra-Music Integration

Dīkṣitar's compositional method was unique in its degree of integration between mantra and music. His process (as reconstructed from the testimony of his students and the internal evidence of his compositions) involved:

  1. Selecting the deity and the mantra: The specific aspect of the divine to be invoked, and the specific mantra (bījākṣara or longer formula) associated with that aspect

  2. Selecting the rāga: Based on the rāga's therapeutic properties, its traditional association with the deity, and its capacity to carry the specific mantra

  3. Constructing the sāhitya: Building the Sanskrit text around the mantra, embedding the rāga name (rāga mudrā), the deity's names and attributes, and specific Tantric terminology

  4. Fusing text and melody: Setting the text to melody in such a way that the phonemic properties of each Sanskrit syllable align with the tonal properties of each musical note — heavy syllables on strong notes, light syllables on light notes, nasal syllables on resonant notes, etc.

This four-fold process ensures that every Dīkṣitar kṛti is a fully integrated healing instrument — mantra, rāga, sāhitya, and melody working in concert to produce a specific therapeutic effect.

The Nine Planets and Their Significance

In Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology), the Navagrahas (nine planets) govern different aspects of human life:

Graha Domain Body System Psychological Quality Disease Pattern
